stages.title: Reading and writing fundamentals
stages.hook: Read the word ספר with no vowel marks. Is it "sefer" (book), "sapar" (barber) or "safar" (he counted)?
explain: Hebrew letters mostly show consonants. Vowels are shown by niqqud, points and dashes under, over or inside letters: patakh and kamatz (both a), tsere and segol (both e), khirik (i), kholam (o), shuruk and kubuts (u). A shva is a very short or silent mark.

Adults normally read without niqqud, using context. Children's books, poetry, prayer books and learner books add them. Some letters also work as vowels: י often shows i or e, and ו shows o or u. Spelling with these helper letters is called "full spelling" (ktiv male).
Final forms are used at the end of words: ך ם ן ף ץ. Printed and handwritten Hebrew differ a lot: handwriting is cursive and the letters look quite different.
stages.mnemonic: Niqqud: tiny helpers under the letter that say which vowel to sing.
sentences: The school is near the house.

gq.q: Which letter can sometimes show the vowel o or u?
gq.why: Vav can serve as a vowel letter.

panel.q: Why can an adult read ספר without niqqud?
o: Context and vocabulary show which word it is
Unpointed words have only one meaning
Unpointed words have only one meaning in Hebrew

panel.q: Which text usually has full niqqud?
panel.why: Learner and children's books use niqqud to teach reading.

panel.q: Why does the unpointed word ספר have more than one possible reading?
panel.model: Without niqqud the same letters can be sefer (book), sapar (barber) or safar (he counted), so context decides.
panel.why: Vowels are not written, so words can share a spelling.

teach.model: Hebrew letters show mainly consonants. Small marks called niqqud show vowels. Adults usually read without them, using context. Children and learners use niqqud.

points.ask: What do the letters mainly show?
How do adults read without them?

stages.title: Basic sentence construction
stages.hook: In English we say "The house is big". In Hebrew we say "The house big". Where did the word "is" go?
explain: A Hebrew sentence often has no word for "is" in the present: ha-bayit gadol, "the house (is) big". The order is usually subject, verb, object: ha-talmid kore et ha-sefer, "the student reads the book".

The little word et comes before a definite direct object: kore et ha-sefer. It is not translated, but it tells you that the next word is the thing receiving the action. With an indefinite object there is no et: kotev mila.

To say "have" Hebrew uses yesh li, "there is to me". The opposite is ein li, "I do not have". Yesh means "there is", ein means "there isn't". When you want "is" with a noun, Hebrew can add hu (he) or hi (she): akhi hu rofe, "my brother is a doctor".
stages.mnemonic: Yesh = there is, ein = there isn't. Two tiny words for have and have not.
sentences: The house is big and new.
My brother is a good doctor.

gq.q: How do you say "I have a dog"?
gq.why: Hebrew says "there is to me a dog".

gq.q: What is the job of "et" in "kore et ha-sefer"?
o: It marks a definite direct object
It means "and" and joins two nouns
gq.why: Et appears before a definite direct object.

panel.q: Which sentence needs "et"?
o: ani ro'e et ha-bayit (I see the house)
ani ro'e bayit (I see a house)
ani ro'e bayit gadol (I see a big house)

panel.q: Why is "ha-mayim karim" plural (karim)?
o: Mayim (water) is a plural noun in Hebrew
Water is cold, so the adjective is plural
panel.why: Mayim is plural in form, so the adjective is plural.

panel.q: How do you say "there is no milk"?

teach.model: Hebrew leaves out is in the present. Use yesh li for I have and ein for there is not. Put et before a definite object.

points.ask: Is there a word for is?
How do I say I have?

stages.title: Common verbs
stages.hook: "I went", "you went", "she went": in Hebrew the end of one verb tells you who did it. Can you spot the clue?
explain: Hebrew past verbs use endings for the person. The base form is the "he" form: katav (he wrote). Add -ti for I (katavti), -ta for you (m) (katavta), -t for you (f) (katavt), -a for she (katva), -nu for we (katavnu).

The pronoun is often not needed, though speakers do say ani halakhti. Many of the commonest verbs belong to one pattern (binyan) called pa'al: katav (wrote), halakh (went), akhal (ate), shata (drank), patakh (opened), yashav (sat), shama (heard), ra'a (saw).
The same root gives the present and future: kotev (writes), yikhtov (will write). Listen to the last sounds of a verb to know who did it.
stages.mnemonic: -ti is me, -ta is you: the ending is the pronoun.
sentences: We opened the window in the morning.

gq.q: Which ending means "I" in the past tense?
What is the past of "to write" for "he"?
gq.why: Katav is the base past form.

panel.q: Why can "halakhti le-beit ha-sefer" omit the word ani?
o: The verb ending already shows the speaker is "I"
Hebrew has no pronouns, so the verb carries them

panel.q: How do you tell katavta (you, m.) from katavt (you, f.)?
o: By the first letter of the verb stem
panel.why: The feminine "you" ends with a bare -t.

panel.q: Which verb form is right for "Dana drank the milk"?
panel.why: A feminine subject takes the feminine past, which adds -a: shatta.

teach.model: Hebrew past verbs end with -ti for I, -ta for you (m), -t for you (f), -nu for we. The pronoun is often not needed.

points.ask: How does the verb show who did it?

stages.title: Nouns, pronouns and modifiers
stages.hook: The word for a male teacher is "more". What small ending do you think a female teacher gets?
explain: Pronouns: ani (I), atah (you, m), at (you, f), hu (he), hi (she), anakhnu (we), hem (they, m), hen (they, f). Nouns are masculine or feminine. A feminine noun often ends in -a or -t: more (male teacher), mora (female teacher).
Plurals end in -im (usually masculine) or -ot (usually feminine): talmid → talmidim, talmida → talmidot. Some masculine nouns take -ot, such as shulkhan → shulkhanot, so learn plurals with the noun.

The adjective follows the noun and must agree in gender, number and definiteness: ha-bayit ha-gadol (the big house) versus ha-bayit gadol (the house is big). In the first the adjective takes ha- as well.

o: ha-bayit gadol, which uses ha- once
gq.why: Both the noun and the adjective take ha-.

gq.q: What is the plural of talmida (female student)?
gq.why: Feminine nouns ending in -a usually take -ot.

panel.q: Why is "ha-bayit gadol" a sentence, not a phrase?
o: The adjective lacks ha-, so it is a predicate
It is plural, so the adjective ends in -im
panel.why: A bare adjective after a definite noun makes a statement.

panel.q: Why is shulkhanot (tables) interesting?
o: A masculine noun takes the usual feminine plural -ot
It is a feminine noun, so the ending is normal

panel.q: What must an adjective agree with in Hebrew?
panel.model: The adjective agrees with the noun in gender and number, and also in definiteness (ha-).

teach.model: Hebrew has pronouns like ani for I and hu for he. Nouns have gender and form plurals with -im or -ot. Adjectives follow nouns and agree with them.

stages.title: Questions and responses
stages.hook: To ask a yes/no question in everyday Hebrew you can just raise your voice. In formal Hebrew there is a word for it. Can you guess?
explain: In speech, a yes/no question uses intonation: atah medaber ivrit? "Do you speak Hebrew?" The formal question word is ha'im: ha'im atah medaber ivrit? Answers are ken (yes) and lo (no).

Question words: mi (who), ma (what), eifo (where), matay (when), eikh (how), lama (why), kama (how much or many). Eifo ha-sifriya? means "where is the library?" Kama ze ole? means "how much does it cost?"
Because the question words are used in school and daily life, practise them with the verbs you know. Questions end with a question mark, and Hebrew uses the same mark as English.
stages.mnemonic: Question words start the sentence; yes/no needs only a rising voice.

gq.q: How do you usually ask a yes/no question in everyday Hebrew?
gq.why: Spoken Hebrew uses intonation; ha'im is more formal.

panel.q: A learner replies to "atah student?" with "eifo". Why is this wrong?
o: A yes/no question needs ken or lo
Eifo means yes, so the answer matches
panel.why: Yes/no questions need yes or no.

panel.q: Where does a question word such as eifo normally go?
panel.why: Question words usually open the sentence.

panel.q: Which question asks "when"?

teach.model: For yes or no, raise your voice, or use the formal ha'im. For information use mi, ma, eifo, matay, eikh, lama and kama.

points.ask: How do I ask a yes/no question?

stages.title: Describing people and places
stages.hook: Describe a friend: tall? kind? funny? In Hebrew, the describing word has to match your friend's gender. What changes?
explain: An adjective comes after the noun and matches it. Masculine: ha-yeled gavoha (the boy is tall). Feminine: ha-yalda gvohah. The plural has -im or -ot: yeladim gvohim, yeladot gvohot.
Common adjectives: gavoha (tall), namukh (short), nekhmad (nice), khakham (smart), gadol (big), katan (small), yafe (beautiful), karov (near). The feminine of yafe is yafa, and the plural is yafim.
To compare, put yoter before the adjective and mi after: yoter gadol mi-... (bigger than ...). Hebrew uses "mi-" (from) for "than".
sentences: The city is big and beautiful.
My teacher is nice and smart.
The park is near my house.

gq.q: "Ir" (city) is feminine. Which phrase is correct for "a big city"?
gq.why: A feminine noun takes the feminine adjective after it.
Yoter + adjective + mi- gives the comparative.

panel.q: What is the plural of "yafe" (beautiful, m.)?
Why do you say "ha-mora khakhama" but "ha-more khakham"?
o: Mora is feminine and more is masculine
Women are cleverer, so the word changes

panel.q: Where does the adjective go in Hebrew, and what must it match?
panel.model: It comes after the noun and agrees in gender and number, and also in definiteness.
panel.why: Hebrew adjectives follow the noun and agree.

teach.model: Hebrew adjectives come after the noun and agree in gender and number. Use yoter and mi- to compare.

stages.title: Time, dates and daily routines
stages.hook: In Israel the working week starts on Sunday. What do you think Sunday is called in Hebrew?
explain: Hebrew days are numbered: yom rishon (day one, Sunday), yom sheni (Monday), yom shlishi (Tuesday), yom revi'i (Wednesday), yom khamishi (Thursday), yom shishi (Friday) and Shabbat (Saturday), the day of rest. In Israel the weekend is Friday and Saturday, with Friday often a half or no working day.

Besides the usual calendar, Israel uses the Hebrew calendar, a lunisolar calendar, for holidays such as Rosh Hashanah. Time: ha-sha'a shva, "the time is seven". A man says ani kam be-sheva (I get up at seven).
For the future, use the future tense: nisa le-yerushalayim ("we will travel to Jerusalem"). Common time words: ha-yom (today), makhar (tomorrow), etmol (yesterday).
stages.mnemonic: Yom rishon, sheni, shlishi: the week counts itself.
sentences: Tomorrow we are travelling to Jerusalem.

o: A lunisolar calendar used for holidays
A solar calendar used only by the army
gq.why: It follows both the Moon and the Sun.

panel.q: Why is Saturday called Shabbat and not "yom shevii"?
o: It is the day of rest, with its own name
It is a mistake that people have copied
panel.why: Shabbat has a special name and meaning.

panel.q: Why do Israeli weekends fall on Friday and Saturday?
o: Shabbat is the day of rest, and Friday is a short workday before it
It is random and has changed every few years

panel.q: What time does "ha-sha'a shva" tell?
o: It is a week with seven days

teach.model: Days are numbered: yom rishon, yom sheni and so on, and Shabbat is the day of rest. Israel also uses the Hebrew calendar for holidays.

stages.title: Food and shopping
stages.hook: In the market people call out prices. Which short question gets the price in Hebrew?
explain: To ask the price say kama ze ole? "How much does this cost?" or kama ole ha-lekhem? Numbers and shekels are used in shops: shekel is the currency. A polite request is ani rotze... "I would like...", with ani rotsa for a woman.
Food words: orez (rice), of (chicken), te (tea), kafe (coffee), temarim (dates), zeitim (olives). Foods like hummus, falafel and challah are well known. Challah is the special bread for Shabbat.
Shopping at an outdoor market (shuk) can include friendly bargaining. Say "yakar" (expensive) or "zol" (cheap). In shops prices are usually fixed.
stages.mnemonic: Kama ze ole? = "how much does it cost?", the first phrase in every shop.
sentences: I would like a cup of tea.
How much does this bread cost?
The coffee is hot and tasty.

gq.why: Kama ze ole means how much does it cost?

o: A kind of coffee served on Shabbat
gq.why: Challah is traditionally eaten on Shabbat.

panel.q: A woman says "ani rotze". What is wrong?
Which reply is a polite way to say a price seems too high?
o: ze zol meod, which means very cheap
panel.why: Saying it is a little expensive starts a negotiation.

panel.q: Why is "kos te" (a cup of tea) used instead of just "te" when ordering?
o: A measure word shows the quantity
Te cannot stand alone as a Hebrew noun
It is a rule for kids
panel.why: Quantity words are used before nouns.

teach.model: Say kama ze ole to ask the price. Say ani rotze to say what you want, or ani rotsa for a woman. Add bevakasha to be polite.

points.ask: How do I ask the price?
How do I say what I want?

stages.title: Everyday conversations
stages.hook: You meet someone new and want to chat. What three questions could you ask first?
explain: A simple talk: ma shimkha? (What is your name?, to a man). Shmi Dan. Me-eifo atah? (Where are you from?) Ani mi-Marokko. Naim le-hakir means "nice to meet you". When someone asks ma nishma? or ma shlomkha? you can say ha-kol be-seder (all is fine), toda.
A friendly Israeli reply may be sababa, "great or cool", slang that comes from Arabic. Slang changes fast. Another common ending is le-hitraot, "see you".
Hebrew used in conversation is Modern Hebrew. Remember to use the right gender: a man says ani medaber ivrit ktsat (I speak a little Hebrew) and a woman says ani medaberet.
stages.mnemonic: Ma nishma? = "what is heard?": a friendly way to ask "what's up?".
items: what is your name? (to a man)
where are you from? (to a man)

gq.why: It is said when meeting someone.

gq.q: Where does the slang word "sababa" come from?

panel.q: Why does a woman say "ani medaberet" and a man "ani medaber"?
o: It depends on age, so older speakers use -et

panel.q: Why is slang risky in a formal setting?
o: It is informal and changes quickly
It is illegal in formal settings

panel.q: Name two things you can ask when meeting someone.
panel.model: You can ask their name (ma shimkha?) and where they are from (me-eifo atah?).

teach.model: Ask ma shimkha for the name and me-eifo atah for where they are from. Say naim le-hakir to say nice to meet you. Use ha-kol be-seder for all is fine.

points.ask: How do I ask a name?
How do I ask where someone is from?
What do I say when asked how I am?
